name: Fluent Bit v5 vs OTel Collector — Progressive Signal Benchmark

title.content: # Fluent Bit v5 vs OpenTelemetry Collector — Progressive Signal Benchmark

intro.content:
A like-for-like benchmark of **Fluent Bit v5.1.1** vs **OpenTelemetry Collector-contrib v0.159.0**, stacking one telemetry signal at a time — **logs → +metrics → +traces → +tail-sampling** — so each tier's delta is the *incremental cost of the added signal*. Each engine ran serially (one live at a time, exporting real signals to Dynatrace) through a **2 h rampup validity gate → 24 h+ soak**, on an Istio 1.29 cluster under otel-demo + hipster-shop load.

**Headline:** Fluent Bit is the lighter engine at **every** tier — ~5× lighter memory on logs, ~11× on the metrics arm, ~41% lighter memory / ~44% lighter CPU at the full signal set — with **zero loss** throughout. The Collector is the *capability* engine on trace ingress (native gRPC vs FB HTTP-only) and per-datapoint metrics. No memory leak in either engine at any tier (all runs tail-flat, ≤1.81% drift).

> ⚠️ **Tier 4 erratum / re-run in progress:** an earlier version said tail sampling is Collector-only. That is wrong — Fluent Bit v5's `sampling` processor (`type: tail`) supports it too. Tier 4 is being re-run as a like-for-like both-engines tail-sampling comparison; the T4 figures below are superseded pending that re-run. Tiers 1–3 unaffected.

narrative.content:
### Incremental cost of each added signal
- **Logs (T1):** both cheap & leak-free over 24–26 h. Fluent Bit ~30% lower CPU, ~5× lower memory, ~30% lower cost/1M at matched ~755 rec/s.
- **+metrics (T1→T2):** a high-cardinality istiod-CP + Kepler scrape on a dedicated metrics StatefulSet. Widest gap of the ladder: Collector metrics pipeline ~**78 MiB** tail-flat vs Fluent Bit ~**7 MiB / 2 m** — **~11× memory advantage** for Fluent Bit. Neither leaks under the Kepler stressor.
- **+traces (T2→T3):** OTLP trace path on a dedicated traces workload. Fluent Bit holds its lead — ~200 MiB vs ~337 MiB, ~100 m vs ~180 m CPU — with **zero dropped** vs the Collector's small non-zero loss (0.011% DT-failed). Trace ingress differs by design (FB HTTP :4318 only vs Collector gRPC :4317).
- **+tail-sampling (T3→T4):** the most expensive single add. On the collector the stateful tailsampling processor (keep-errors OR 30% probabilistic non-health, decision_wait 10 s, num_traces 100k) pushes the traces pod **53 → 152 MiB (~2.9×)**. Both engines support tail sampling (FB v5 `sampling` `type: tail`); the like-for-like both-engines re-run is in progress — these T4 figures are the collector-only-TS run.

ts_md.content:
### 🎯 Tier 4 — tail-sampling cost (re-run in progress)
The tail-sampling stage is *stateful* — it buffers trace windows before deciding — so it costs memory: on the collector the traces pod grows **~2.9×** and the decision buffer rides its 100k-trace cap the whole soak (still tail-flat at **+0.00%**).

**Correction:** Fluent Bit v5 also supports tail sampling (`sampling` `type: tail`) — the original run mistakenly configured it collector-only. Tier 4 is being re-run with **both** engines sampling so the cost comparison is like-for-like; the figures here are from the collector-only-TS run and are superseded.

sec_live.content:
## 📈 Rampup → soak — live Dynatrace time-series (real Grail data)
Overlaid from each engine's actual Tier-4 run window, aligned by relative interval (the OTAP-benchmark compare technique). Default window = the **2 h rampup**; widen the **Duration** variable (hours) to view into the soak. `avg` = per-container mean across the engine's workloads; the tables above carry the authoritative multi-pod totals.

live_cpu.title: CPU during the run — Collector vs Fluent Bit (avg container mCores)
live_cpu.query:
timeseries base=avg(dt.kubernetes.container.cpu_usage), filter:{ matchesValue(k8s.cluster.name,$K8sCluster) and matchesValue(k8s.workload.name,"bench-collector-*") }, from:toTimestamp($collector), to:toTimestamp($collector)+duration(toLong($Duration),unit:"h"), interval:5m | fieldsAdd collector=base[] | fieldsRemove base
| lookup [ timeseries r=avg(dt.kubernetes.container.cpu_usage), filter:{ matchesValue(k8s.cluster.name,$K8sCluster) and matchesValue(k8s.workload.name,"bench-fluentbit-*") }, from:toTimestamp($fluentbit), to:toTimestamp($fluentbit)+duration(toLong($Duration),unit:"h"), interval:5m | fieldsAdd fluentbit=r[] | fieldsRemove r ], sourceField:interval, lookupField:interval, fields:{fluentbit}

sec_rampup.content:
## ✅ Rampup validation — incoming cluster log volume climbs with the load (real Grail data)
The test is only valid if the load actually ramped. These tiles show **incoming log records per 5 min across the whole cluster** over each engine's 2 h rampup window — a rising curve confirms the 50→200 VU/app ramp drove real traffic. Windows follow the `collector` / `fluentbit` variables; widen `Duration` to see the soak plateau.

rampup_col.title: Incoming cluster logs during the 2h rampup (records / 5 min) — climbing curve validates the load ramp
rampup_col.query: fetch logs, from:toTimestamp($collector), to:toTimestamp($collector)+duration(toLong($Duration),unit:"h") | filter matchesValue(k8s.cluster.name,$K8sCluster) | makeTimeseries incoming_logs=count(), interval:5m

footer.content:
### Reproduce this benchmark
Engine pins, pipeline configs (both engines, all four tiers), the load harness, and the full step-by-step run guide (2 h rampup → 24 h soak) are in the repository. Methodology follows the serial single-engine pattern: deploy one engine → validate signal received + census 0-restart + load reaching the app → rampup gate → soak → tear down → next engine.
